# docs_audit_report — 2026-07-25

## TL;DR (stranger's 30-second take)
The hero explains Carnot, but I would close the tab once the page turns into an internal research dashboard full of unexplained benchmarks, release archaeology, and suspiciously perfect results. The MIT-0/Apache-2.0 contradiction is an immediate credibility failure.

## TOP 3 PROBLEMS
1. The license contradicts itself — “MIT-0” in the hero and metadata vs “Apache 2.0 License” in the footer.
2. “What we measured” is a 12-card wall of unexplained acronyms and incomparable metrics with almost no inspectable evidence.
3. The hero and preprint sections read like internal status reporting — 382 milestones, “repinned from v2,” “paper-v6,” and a pending operator upload.

## DETAILED FINDINGS
### Bloat
- Navigation — 12 text links plus 2 platform buttons — cap at roughly 5 primary destinations.
- Hero stats — 4 counters plus a roughly 47-word “Recent progress” card — cap at 2–3 decision-relevant proof points; experiment and milestone totals are vanity metrics.
- “What we measured” — 12 result cards — cap at 3–5 comparable headline results, with the remainder behind an evidence link.
- “From the blog” — 7 cards — cap at 3 recent or foundational posts.
- Results plus blog sections — 19 consecutive cards — enough visual repetition that a stranger will stop reading individual cards.
- “Why Energy-Based?” — approximately 72 words — under the 120-word hard limit, but too long and speculative for an explanatory card; cap at roughly 45 words.
- Bento cards — none appears to exceed 120 words — the problem is cumulative density and scope drift, not an individual hard-limit violation.
- Result cards — none appears to exceed 60 words — their brevity does not help because context needed to interpret the numbers is missing.
- Footer paragraph — under 100 words — no bloat violation.

### Internal jargon
- Hero statistics and “Recent progress” — “FoVer,” “AUROC,” “5-seed dual-condition,” “architecture-only,” and “v2 0.9857” — a newcomer cannot identify the dataset, conditions, or why three AUROCs appear.
- “Why Energy-Based?” — “gradient,” “FPGA Ising machines,” and “thermodynamic samplers” — unexplained technical escalation unrelated to the initial use case.
- “Typed constraints” — “CCTU constrained tool-use micro-benchmark” — neither CCTU nor the benchmark is explained.
- “APIs & portable memory” — “MCP,” `VerdictRecord`, and `SessionMemory` — internal API names are presented as benefits without explaining the user problem they solve.
- “Test-Time Compute (TTC) & PREM” — TTC and “Process-Reward Energy Model” are introduced without explaining what the feature actually checks; “intrinsic motivation for continuous self-learning” is research jargon, not product language.
- Results — “KV260,” “Ising,” “SVAMP,” “AUC,” “FoVer,” “CRANE,” “CoT,” “VeriCoT,” “PRM-BiasBench,” “k=5,” “HalluGuard v3,” and “pp” — nearly every card assumes prior project or research knowledge.
- Preprint — “paper-v6,” “checked-in experiment artifacts,” “non-operator environment,” and “operator-initiated upload” — repository/process language exposed to the public.
- Blog cards — “NTK,” an unexplained arXiv identifier, “30B,” and “AUROCs” — titles and summaries presume research-insider context.

### Per-milestone narrative
- Hero statistics — “382 Completed milestones” — internal project throughput is not a reason to adopt the product.
- “Recent progress” — “Repinned from v2 0.9857 after pre-submission adversarial audit” — release archaeology that forces a stranger to reconstruct why the old number was wrong.
- Preprint — “Carnot position paper (paper-v6)” — an internal draft identifier masquerading as a public title.
- Preprint — “The arXiv submission is prepared but pending operator-initiated upload” — an internal to-do item, not landing-page copy.
- “Research operations” — planner/inner-agent/adversarial-verify artifact workflow — describes how the project runs itself, not what a user can accomplish.
- “Two Retractions and a Rescue,” “Regex in an NTK Costume,” and “Caught Cheating” — the cumulative story is dominated by internal failures and remediation rather than user outcomes.
- No raw `Exp 1688`-style or `.148`-style identifiers appear, but `paper-v6`, `v2`, milestone totals, and submission status create the same internal-reporting effect.

### Inconsistencies
- “MIT-0 · Open Source” and metadata saying “MIT-0” vs footer saying “Apache 2.0 License.”
- “Seven capabilities” under “What you can check” vs cards for research operations, integration surfaces, and a compute-budget controller, none of which is a type of output Carnot checks.
- “No model fine-tuning required” vs a headline result for “Two-GPU parallel retrain”; these may refer to different workflows, but the page never distinguishes product usage from research infrastructure.
- FoVer verifier AUROC `0.9131` vs architecture-only `0.8947` vs withdrawn/repinned `0.9857` vs a `0.125 FoVer baseline` on the SVAMP card. These may not be directly comparable, but the page presents them without enough definitions to prevent apparent contradiction.
- The Python tab demonstrates answer verification and repair, while the Rust tab demonstrates low-level Ising energy and Langevin sampling. They are labeled as parallel quick-start options but do not perform equivalent tasks.

### Missing essentials
- What Carnot does is present: the hero says it checks an LLM answer for internal consistency and suggests a repair.
- Installation is present through `pip install carnot-ebm` and a Python example, but there is no direct PyPI package link, version, requirements, or CPU/GPU expectation.
- Trust is asserted rather than demonstrated. Result cards lack direct artifact links, sample sizes, confidence intervals, model versions, evaluation dates, and benchmark protocols.
- The claimed independent reproduction is anonymous: “a non-operator environment” does not identify who reproduced it or where the reproduction record can be inspected.
- The license is effectively missing because the two displayed answers conflict.
- “Ian Blenke” appears as a copyright holder, but the page does not clearly state who maintains Carnot, whether there is a team or organization, or how to contact maintainers.
- There is no clear maturity/status statement telling a stranger whether this is experimental research software or a production-ready verifier.

### Fabrication signals
- “GSM8K extraction TP rate: 0.5 → 1.0” — perfect endpoint with no sample size, false-positive rate, or protocol.
- “k=5 ensemble catches 60/60 attacks” — perfect result on a small, possibly project-authored attack set with no independence or uncertainty anchor.
- “99.3% of wrong code flagged” on 164 HumanEval problems — near-perfect detection without counts, confidence intervals, or false-positive rate.
- “Zero false positives” in “Carnot Dogfooding by the Numbers” — perfect self-evaluation claim embedded in promotional copy.
- “2.0× speedup, identical losses” — suspiciously exact equivalence without hardware, repetitions, variance, or tolerance.
- “0.0pp accuracy delta with 4.4% cost savings” — exact zero degradation without dataset size or uncertainty.
- Multiple 100%-width meters — visually imply perfection even when the associated claim is hardware availability or training speedup rather than a percentage.
- “5,248 experiment runs,” “382 completed milestones,” and “30,658 automated tests” — large exact counts create activity theater but provide no evidence that Carnot works for a stranger’s workload.
- “Externally reproducible” — overstates the credibility of one unidentified clean-checkout recomputation.

## WHAT'S WORKING
- The hero gives a plain-language explanation of Carnot and a concrete wrong-arithmetic example.
- The install command and short Python verification example make the intended workflow tangible.

## RECOMMENDED OPERATOR ACTIONS
1. Resolve the license contradiction everywhere before making any other credibility claim.
2. Reduce the hero to the one-sentence value proposition, install CTA, and at most two independently understandable proof points.
3. Replace the 12-card evidence wall with 3–5 comparable results that include dataset, sample size, baseline, model, uncertainty, and direct artifact links.
4. Remove milestone counts, `paper-v6`, `v2` repinning history, pending-upload status, and other internal operations language from the landing page.
5. Expand or remove every unexplained acronym; delete cards whose benefit cannot be stated without project-specific vocabulary.
6. Separate user-facing capabilities from research infrastructure, integrations, and speculative hardware work.
7. Make the Rust quick start demonstrate the same verify/repair outcome as Python, or label it explicitly as a low-level sampler example.
8. Add an authoritative license link, maintainer/team statement, support/contact route, maturity warning, and direct PyPI link.
9. Qualify perfect and near-perfect numbers with sample sizes, denominators, false-positive rates, uncertainty, and evaluation provenance.
10. Cut the blog preview to three posts and lead with practical use cases instead of the project’s internal audit drama.
